title: Unit – 1 : Session – 2 : SLO – 1  |  Digital systems and number systems
sections: 1. Synchronous sequential systems update their state only at fixed clock intervals (clock-driven, easier to design and debug); asynchronous systems change state whenever inputs change (no clock, faster but prone to race conditions and harder to analyze).
2. A binary signal is a signal that can take only one of two discrete values (0 or 1). Physical examples: voltage levels 0 V / +5 V in a circuit; switch OFF/ON; magnetic polarity on a storage disk.
Suitable system: a synchronous SEQUENTIAL digital system (a counter built from flip-flops).
State: the current count is stored in flip-flops (internal state with memory). Input: count pulses from the wheel sensor and a reset line. Output: the state drives the odometer display.

Synchronous is justified because all flip-flops update together on a common clock edge, so the count changes cleanly and predictably with no race conditions; an asynchronous ripple counter could show transient wrong values. A synchronous counter with a clear/reset input meets the precise-tracking and reset requirements.
Synchronous System — d) Updates at fixed intervals
Asynchronous System — e) Updates at any time
A basic calculator uses BOTH: combinational logic (adders/ALU that compute results from current inputs) and sequential logic (registers/memory that hold operands and running totals).
Components: (i) Inputs — keypad; (ii) Outputs — display; (iii) Memory/state — registers storing the first operand and intermediate result.

Classification logic: the arithmetic unit alone is combinational (output depends only on present inputs), but storing numbers between key presses requires state, making the overall calculator a sequential system.
